keyVerseText: Return, return, O Shulamite; return, return, that we may look upon thee. What will ye see in the Shulamite? As it were the company of two armies. of: or, of Mahanaim
rootMeaning: The word שׁוּלַמִּית (Shûwlammîyth) derives from the Hebrew root שָׁלַם (shâlam), which conveys ideas of completeness, peace, and restoration. This root encompasses notions of making amends, being whole or perfect, and experiencing peace both inwardly and outwardly. Thus, the literal sense of Shulamite as "the perfect" or "the peaceful" adds a rich dimension beyond a mere proper name, suggesting a character marked by wholeness and tranquility.
usageInScripture: The term שׁוּלַמִּית appears only twice in Scripture, consistently translated as "O Shulamite," highlighting the personal and intimate nature of the term as a proper noun. It is used specifically as an epithet for the heroine lover in the Song of Songs, indicating her identity as the beloved and emphasizing her unique qualities. This consistent usage underscores the word's role in conveying both a personal name and a poetic title that embodies peace and perfection.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding שׁוּלַמִּית as rooted in the concept of peace and perfection enriches our appreciation of the Song of Songs and its portrayal of love. The Shulamite, as the beloved, symbolizes the ideal of harmonious relationship and restored fellowship, themes that resonate deeply with the Christian faith's emphasis on reconciliation through Christ. This name invites believers to see the beauty of perfected love and peace as reflections of God's redemptive work, pointing ultimately to the Church's relationship with Christ as the bridegroom who brings true peace and wholeness.
keyVerseReflection: In Song of Solomon 6:13, the repeated call "Return, return, O Shulamite; return, return, that we may look upon thee" highlights the beloved's central place in the community's gaze and affection. The use of "Shulamite" here emphasizes her identity as the peaceful and perfect one, whose presence is as formidable and harmonious as "the company of two armies." This word thus deepens the verse's meaning by portraying the Shulamite not only as an object of desire but also as a symbol of strength and unity in love.
